sentences.text: Hallopus was a small animal reaching about 1 meter (3.3 feet) in length, though comparisons with other sphenosuchians estimate its body length at approximately 62 cm.

The humerus of Hallopus was hollow, as shown by impressions and the preserved distal end of the bone, and its structure suggests the animal could stretch its forearms into a straight line with the upper arm bone. This ratio of the humerus to the combined radius and radiale is 146%, a proportion only exceeded by giraffes, while relatively stiff wrist joints effectively increased the length of its forearms.

Evidence suggests Hallopus walked on its toes with its forelimbs, supported by the distribution of length in its finger bones. It likely walked on its hind toes with three effective toes that were locked together at the base before spreading at the tips. Hallopus had long feet where the central toe bones were about as long as the metatarsals, and the entire foot was roughly the same length as the tibia. The narrow heel of Hallopus lacked a groove found in modern crocodiles, suggesting it functioned like a lever similar to cursorial mammals.
The name Hallopus comes from the Greek words for "jumping" and "foot".
Its arm bone proportions are so extreme that the ratio of the humerus to the combined radius and radiale is 146%, a proportion only exceeded by giraffes.
The narrow heel of Hallopus lacked a groove found in modern crocodiles, suggesting it functioned like a lever similar to cursorial mammals.

Hallopus was originally described as a dinosaur species named Nanosaurus victor in 1877 before being reclassified into its own genus in 1881. The holotype fossil was found near Canyon City, Colorado, and purchased by collector Baldwin for three dollars at a shop in Colorado Springs. The holotype consists of two rock slabs holding largely separated remains of a single individual, including spine and limb elements.

Charles Schuchert suggested in 1939 that Hallopus was found in the upper members of the Morrison Formation based on letters between Marsh and the collector. A full, detailed description of Hallopus was published in 1890, with revisions continuing throughout the 1890s. O. C. Marsh classified Hallopus as a dinosaur in 1881 based on bones he initially identified as a pubis, which von Huene later reinterpreted as an ischium. Additional fossils found include a femur, functionally tridactyl foot bones, and a humerus. The genus Hallopus was named by Marsh in 1881.

Walker proposed that Hallopus used a strutting gait where the forelimbs strutted while the anterior body bounced to increase stride length. A long tail, inferred from relatives and recovered caudal vertebrae, would have significantly affected Hallopus's movement.

The lack of relevant skull material leaves Hallopus's diet ambiguous. The teeth of the related Macelognathus are unserrated and flattened, suggesting a diet of insects and plant material rather than meat.

Hallopus is classified as a small sphenosuchian crocodylomorph. Hallopus was considered a dinosaur for nearly a century until its crocodylomorph relationships were recognized in the 1970s. Walker identified anatomical details establishing Hallopus as a pseudosuchian, less derived than Protosuchus or Orthosuchus.

A 2017 phylogenetic analysis placed Hallopus in the clade Hallopodidae with Macelognathus and Almadasuchus. Ruebenstahl and colleagues found Hallopus to be a sister taxon to Solidocrania, a clade containing Macelognathus, Junggarsuchus, and Almadasuchus.

Hallopus lived during the Late Jurassic in the Morrison Formation of North America. Research by Ague, Carpenter, and Ostrom in 1995 confirmed the existence of Upper Morrison sediments around "The Nipple" where Hallopus was found. Hallopus is a prehistoric possible sphenosuchian reptile found in Garden Park, Colorado, USA, in Upper Jurassic sediments. Hallopus lived during the Tithonian stage, between 149.2 and 145.06 million years ago.

Marsh initially classified Hallopus within Dinosauria in 1881 but later doubted this, suggesting it might be a link between dinosaurs and primitive forms like aetosaurs or crocodilians. The similarity between Hallopus and Macelognathus has led to recent taxonomic debates regarding whether they are distinct or synonymous. Leardi and colleagues suggest Hallopus and Macelognathus may be synonymous, but this requires closer inspection of the holotype or additional material to confirm. The lack of well-preserved cranial material makes Hallopus's exact phylogenetic position uncertain.
